patterns_data.top_pattern: Authorization classification and unmapped facility shifts need validation before action
patterns_data.what_is_impacting: Medicaid inpatient authorization classification and facility mapping across FL, CA, IN / MD / MO, and IA
key_driver_codes: Degenerative Nervous System Disorders with MCC
Vaginal Delivery with O.R. Procedures Except Sterilization and/or D&C
patterns_data.pattern_details: A large share of the identified increase is tied to authorization-classification movement rather than a clean utilization or price story. FL, CA, and IN / MD / MO all show the same authorization distribution issue, and IA adds a separate facility mapping problem through a Not Mapped bucket. These items should be treated as gating validation work before changing UM, reimbursement, or network strategy.
patterns_data.why_it_matters: If these records are misclassified, business actions taken on them could target the wrong providers, products, or utilization levers.
patterns_data.recommended_next_step: Run a focused validation of authorization-to-claim mapping and facility mapping in FL, CA, IN / MD / MO, and IA, then restate the impacted spend before making policy or provider interventions.
patterns_data.validation_reason: The source groups are explicitly flagged for authorization or mapping shifts, including AUTH_CODE_DISTRIBUTION and an unmapped facility bucket that require validation before action.
evidence_summary: FL authorization classification shifts account for about $58.1M and are flagged for validation before action.
CA shows another $18.3M with the same authorization classification issue, centered in neurologic and back-related inpatient cases.
IN / MD / MO add about $12.6M, including Riley's Children's Health and delivery and behavioral health cases.
IA adds about $3.4M in LTSS Dual Eligible spend tied to a Not Mapped facility bucket and no-auth claims, indicating a separate mapping problem.

patterns_data.top_pattern: FL free-standing SNF growth is the largest real utilization driver
patterns_data.what_is_impacting: FL Medicaid free-standing SNF spend for LTSS Dual Eligible and LTSS Non Dual members
key_driver_codes: Degenerative Nervous System Disorders with MCC
patterns_data.pattern_details: FL free-standing SNF spend rose sharply, driven mainly by more admissions rather than a broad spike in unit prices. The increase is concentrated in LTSS Dual Eligible members, with additional growth in LTSS Non Dual. Neurologic and back-related cases appear repeatedly, so the business lever is tighter control of SNF entry, stay management, and discharge planning.
patterns_data.why_it_matters: This is the largest non-validation cost pattern and points to a major site-of-care and utilization management opportunity in FL Medicaid.
patterns_data.recommended_next_step: Launch a FL SNF action plan for LTSS products that reviews admission appropriateness, length-of-stay management, and high-volume SNF provider performance under existing authorization rules.
evidence_summary: FL LTSS Dual Eligible free-standing SNFs added about $61.3M, including 6,568 more admissions and 10,981 more claims.
FL LTSS Non Dual free-standing SNFs added about $8.1M with 853 more admissions.
A smaller but related FL SNF pressure point added about $1.1M in Medical Back Problems without MCC, showing some added unit-cost pressure inside the larger volume story.

Operational paid per admit is often flat or down, which reinforces that more case flow and case mix are the main drivers.
patterns_data.why_it_matters: This pattern points to a targeted clinical and site-of-care management opportunity in CA rather than a general pricing problem.
patterns_data.recommended_next_step: Pair clinical review with SNF/NF utilization management in CA, focusing on neurologic and spine-related admission patterns, post-acute placement decisions, and provider-level discharge pathways.

CA LTSS Dual Eligible free-standing SNFs added about $6.0M with 509 more admissions while paid per admit was slightly down.
CA LTSS Non Dual free-standing SNFs added about $4.9M with 464 more admissions and lower paid per admit, again pointing to volume over price.
CA TANF Standard free-standing SNFs added about $1.9M with 192 more admissions.

patterns_data.top_pattern: Tampa General is a concentrated FL acute-hospital cost driver
patterns_data.what_is_impacting: FL Medicaid acute hospital spend, concentrated at TAMPA GENERAL HOSPITAL
key_driver_codes: Extreme Immaturity or Respiratory Distress Syndrome, Neonate
patterns_data.pattern_details: FL acute-hospital cost pressure is concentrated at Tampa General Hospital, especially in ABD Non Dual members. The pattern includes both higher admission volume and meaningful paid-per-admission increases, which makes this more than a simple utilization issue. A smaller NICU concentration adds additional high-cost intensity at the same provider.
patterns_data.why_it_matters: Provider concentration creates a clearer lever for contract, reimbursement, and level-of-care review than a broad market-wide response.
patterns_data.recommended_next_step: Conduct a Tampa General provider review that combines contract terms, case severity, NICU level-of-care, and UM escalation rules for ABD Non Dual and TANF Standard acute admissions.
evidence_summary: FL ABD Non Dual acute hospitals added about $5.9M with 422 more admissions.
Tampa General Hospital added about $2.2M of ABD Non Dual acute-hospital spend with only 27 more admissions, implying roughly $9.9K higher paid per admit.
Tampa General TANF Standard acute-hospital cases added about $336K through 63 more admissions.
A smaller Tampa General NICU concentration added about $547K across 3 admissions, with about $103.6K higher paid per admit.

patterns_data.why_it_matters: A single-provider concentration can move spend quickly and is more actionable than a diffuse statewide trend.
patterns_data.recommended_next_step: Open a Riley-focused review of admission mix, outlier service lines, and reimbursement terms across TANF Standard and Family Care children's business.
evidence_summary: Riley's Children's Health drove about $7.3M in IN TANF Standard children's facility spend, with 99 more admissions and about $4.9K higher paid per admit.
IN Family Care children's facility added about $1.0M at the same provider, with 19 more admissions and about $2.9K higher paid per admit.

patterns_data.top_pattern: NC behavioral health and acute psych spend is rising on both volume and intensity
patterns_data.what_is_impacting: NC Medicaid acute psych and inpatient behavioral health
patterns_data.pattern_details: North Carolina behavioral health costs increased through a combination of more admissions and materially higher paid per admission. The operational pressure is centered in acute psych for TANF Foster Care, while the clinical side is concentrated in PTSD, adjustment disorder, and stress-related inpatient behavioral health cases. A small rare-case component is also present, so some of the increase is volatile even though the broader trend is real.
patterns_data.why_it_matters: Behavioral health growth driven by both utilization and intensity can accelerate quickly and often needs coordinated clinical, UM, and reimbursement action.
patterns_data.recommended_next_step: Run a North Carolina behavioral health workup that combines acute-psych admission criteria, length-of-stay management, and reimbursement review for high-cost behavioral health episodes.
patterns_data.validation_reason: Part of the increase comes from low-baseline, small-count behavioral health cases that should be clinically validated before broader action is taken.
evidence_summary: NC TANF Foster Care acute psych added about $1.9M with 46 more admissions and roughly $41.2K higher paid per admit.
NC IP BH cases for PTSD and adjustment disorder added about $1.5M with 53 more admissions combined and paid per admit up roughly $7.6K to $19.1K.
Rare stress and OCD behavioral health cases added another about $488K on just 12 admissions, making part of the signal small-N and volatile.

patterns_data.pattern_details: Delivery-related spend is showing a focused cross-state pattern rather than broad hospital inflation. Maryland has the clearest clinical concentration through obstetric complications and higher-paid delivery episodes, while MD, IN, NY, KS, and MO also show acute-hospital delivery pressure tied to vaginal delivery cases with O.R. procedures. The common business lever is maternity episode management and payment logic review.
patterns_data.why_it_matters: Maternity episodes have distinct clinical and reimbursement actions, so they should not be buried inside general acute-hospital trends.
patterns_data.recommended_next_step: Target a maternity episode review for delivery cases with O.R. procedures and obstetric complications, including severity coding, reimbursement logic, and clinical pathways for higher-acuity deliveries.
evidence_summary: MD obstetric delivery and newborn cases added about $572K, led by post-term pregnancy and severe pre-eclampsia, with paid per admit up about $4.1K and $3.1K.
Acute-hospital delivery episodes also rose in MD ($335K), IN ($295K), NY ($345K), KS ($258K), and MO ($246K).
The recurring driver was vaginal delivery with O.R. procedures, pointing to a focused maternity episode pattern.

patterns_data.top_pattern: Behavioral health pressure extends into MO and smaller acute-psych markets
patterns_data.what_is_impacting: MO, NY, and WV Medicaid behavioral health and acute psych
key_driver_codes: MAJ DEPRESS D/O SINGLE EPIS UNS
patterns_data.pattern_details: Missouri shows a meaningful behavioral health pattern across both clinical IP BH cases and acute-hospital operational spend, especially depressive and other neuroses. Smaller but similar acute-psych increases are also present in NY and WV, where higher paid per admit is part of the story. Together, these indicate broader behavioral health pressure outside North Carolina, though at lower scale.
patterns_data.why_it_matters: Recurring behavioral health cost growth across multiple markets supports a targeted BH management strategy instead of isolated one-off responses.
patterns_data.recommended_next_step: Expand behavioral health review beyond NC to MO first, then validate whether NY and WV need tighter acute-psych UM rules or provider payment review for depressive and neurosis admissions.
evidence_summary: MO IP BH cases for major depression and unspecified depression added about $1.6M with 100 more admissions combined and paid per admit up about $4.1K to $4.6K.
MO acute-hospital behavioral health cases added about $1.3M, led by depressive and other neuroses with 84 more admissions and roughly $1.9K to $2.9K higher paid per admit.
Smaller acute-psych spikes also appeared in NY ($451K) and WV ($408K), both tied to depressive episodes and higher paid per admit.
